catalog_quote: A syllable in Nias has the form (C)V, where V may be bimoraic. ... a phonological word is a root plus any string of syllables over which primary stress has influence. ... All words in Nias have the potential to be stressed on the penultimate syllable, apart from a small number of words which have fixed stress on the final syllable (see 2.8 below). The primary indicator of stress in a word in isolation is the auditory loudness of the syllable compared with others. Vowel length and pitch change usually accompany stressed syllables, but are not essential. There does not seem to be any regular assignment of any stress to other syllables in a word. ... Suffixes, both pronominal and derivational, are counted as syllables for the assignment of stress. new_statements.translation: 2.2.3 Suprasegmental phonemes. As we know, suprasegmental phonemes consist of stress, pitch (tone), juncture (pause) and length that are functional in nature, i.e. able to distinguish meaning. After investigating, it turns out that in BN [bahasa Nias] there is only one suprasegmental phoneme, namely juncture (pause) within the sentence.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's fixed: penultimate syllable record (penultimate stress from catalog-all-2026-09-12, i.e. Brown's Nias Selatan): a non-phonemic (predictable) stress is what a fixed penult rule implies. The work adds only the explicit claim that stress, tone and length are non-contrastive; it gives no placement, so it neither confirms nor challenges 'penult' specifically. Note the dialect difference (see the note on which variety): this book describes general/standard Nias written in Gunungsitoli (northern) forms, not Nias Selatan.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only statement on stress in the book: stress (tekanan), tone (nada) and length are NOT phonemic (not meaning-distinguishing) in Nias; the sole distinctive suprasegmental is sentence-level juncture/pause (illustrated with a minimal pair of sentences differing in pause placement, 'Me mofano ia / isa'a-sa'ai gahenia asu'). No statement anywhere in the book of where word stress falls (the whole text has a single occurrence of 'tekanan'; no 'aksen', no syllable-position statement). 'unclear' here means placement not stated, not that the source is contradictory. Sec. 1.4 (p. 3-5) adds only that the Nias dialects differ in 'intonasi dan cara pengucapannya' (intonation and manner of pronunciation), citing Zagoto 1975.
new_statements.exceptions: none; no stress placement discussed at all
new_statements.identity_note: Glottocode nias1242 is the whole Nias language; the catalog record is named 'Nias Selatan' (the southern variety of Teluk Dalam / Batu Islands, Brown's description). Halawa et al. 1983 describe 'bahasa Nias' (BN) as a whole without naming a base dialect, but their example forms are the Gunungsitoli/northern standard (heza 'ke mana', hadia 'apa', ya'odo/ndra'odo 'saya'), and their own sec. 1.4 (pp. 3-5) distinguishes five dialects (utara: Alasa/Lahewa; kota Gunungsitoli; barat: Mandrehe/Sirombu/Hinako; tengah: Lolowa'u-Gido-Gomo-Lahusa; selatan: Teluk Dalam, Pulau Tello, Pulau-pulau Batu), noting that Teluk Dalam speech sounds 'cepat dan keras' and says haega go moi ndra'ugo where Gunungsitoli says heza moi'o. So the non-phonemic-stress statement is made for standard (northern) Nias, a different dialect from the catalog's Nias Selatan, though the same glottocode language.

audit.reasoning: The classification (penultimate stress in the root+suffix phonological word, prefixes outside the domain, weight-blind (C)V syllables, no regular secondary stress, closed listed set of 14 final-stress words) rests on the best available description, a 613-page fieldwork reference grammar (Brown 2001) that we hold as an open PDF, and every part of the deciding quotation, the exception list and the word-vs-clause domain contrast was re-found verbatim at the stated sections/pages. Glottolog lists no competing grammar or phonology; web search found no instrumental or prosodic study of Nias stress. The only loose end is external: StressTyp2's 'P;U' for 'Nias; Batu' (probably from Sundermann 1913, northern dialect, or reflecting the lexical final-stress set), which does not bear on the southern-dialect coding. Minor identity note: the record's name 'Nias Selatan' is a dialect label under the la

sources.quote: Durch Veränderung der Betonung eines Wortes kann auch eine Conjunction ausgedrückt werden, z. B. chöra = ihnen, chörā = ihnen ober [sic, = aber], ihnen dagegen.
sources.note: Sole stress passage in the work. No statement of the default stress position anywhere: the sound section 'I. Laute und Buchstaben' (pp. 95-96, p. 4) covers letters, the back-throat o, w, z, g, ch and the diphthongs and says nothing about accent; the errata (pp. 349-350) add nothing. The one datum is a minimal pair: chöra 'to them' vs chörā (macron on the final a in print) 'to them however / on the other hand', i.e. a shift of 'Betonung' to the final syllable carries an adversative-conjunction meaning. This adds a grammatical (contrastive) use of stress shift not recorded in the catalog ent

sources.quote: Die allgemeine Regel im Niassischen ist, dass der Ton auf der paenultima liegt: baru, faja, falimösa, fangefa'ö u. s. w. Erhalt das Wort einen Zusatz (etwa ein Suffix) so tritt der Ton wieder auf die Paenultima: barúgu, barunía. Indessen giebt es von dieser Regel manche Ausnahmen und zwar a) liegt der Ton auf der ultima bei den meisten zweisilbigen Adjectiven, resp. Verben, wie aró, anau, ara, mané und manö u. s. w., bei den zweisilbigen Pronomen: ja'ó, andré und andrö, da'é und da'ö und niha in dem Pronomen interrogativum, ha niha? Ausserdem hat <mi> stets den Ton, sowohl im Pronomen: ja'amí (amí), als auch als Suffix: omomí, und ebenso das Suffix mö, barumö. Ferner bei den Verben mit einsilbigem Stamme, wie molí, me'ë, faböi, mondröi, faroi u. s. w. [...] b) auf der antepaenultima bei den Wörtern, die auf eu und iu endigen (welche Laute man also als Halbdiphthonge ansehen könnte) wenn dieselben ein Suffix erhalten, z. B.: fatíusa von fatíu; ëuma von ëu. Bei manchen Wörtern kann auch der Ton bei derselben Form des Wortes bald auf der einen und bald auf der andern Silbe liegen, wodurch dann die Bedeutung eine andere wird, z. B. bóngi = Nacht, es wird Nacht, es ist Nacht; bongí = he
